summary: Chatterjee et al. show that a processor's local memory access sequence for a regular section under a cyclic(k) distribution with affine alignment is produced by a finite state machine with at most k states. They give table-construction algorithms, extend the method to multidimensional arrays, and reuse the same tables to generate shift and stride-change communication sets.
why_read: It explains how HPF-style local addressing and message sets reduce to small per-processor tables, which is a core problem for any data-parallel compiler.
main_contribution: A finite-state-machine formulation of local address sequences and communication sets for cyclic(k) distributions with affine alignment and regular sections.
main_limitation: No O(k) table algorithm is known to the authors, the stride-change case uses a simpler fallback without a stated bound, and the evaluation is a single DAXPY kernel on one workstation.
evaluation_method: Single-processor DAXPY timing over strides and block sizes, preprocessing time against block size, and table-generation and run-time overhead for shift and stride-change communication sets on 32 processors.
benchmarks: DAXPY over regular sections y(l:n:s) on a Sparcstation 2, block sizes 1, 17, 64 and block
Shift and stride-change communication set generation (32 processors)
